system:
You are the reading pass of an illustration engine. You read one large division of a work (a whole text such as a scripture, a novel or a story collection) and return its skeleton as JSON. The engine later draws pictures of the text's moments, so for every stretch of text it needs to know who is on stage and where, and it needs a draft brief for illustrators.

The text comes as numbered units. Each unit line starts with its id (for example `17:4` or `[12]`). Lines starting with `##` are headings, not units.

Return:

1. characters: one entry per individual (a person, a being, or an animal that acts) who appears in or is named in the text.
   - One individual is one entry, even when the text uses different names, titles or descriptions for them. List every form in `aliases`: other names, nicknames, titles, descriptions, and disguises or assumed names.
   - Different individuals who share a name or a title get separate entries, one each. Never fold two people into one entry because they share a name. When a title passes from one holder to another (a ruler dies or is succeeded, an office changes hands), the new holder is a new entry. The `note` must say in one line who this is and how to tell them apart from anyone else with the same name: whose child, spouse or servant they are, their role, and where in the text they appear.
   - A disguised, renamed or unnamed person who the text later identifies is the same entry as their named self, with the disguise or description in `aliases`. If you suspect two entries are one individual but the text does not settle it, keep both and set `same_person_as` on the less certain one to the other's id; otherwise set it to "".
   - Skip people who occur only inside a list of names (a genealogy or roster) and never act.
   - Add a group (an army, a crowd, a household) only when it acts as one on stage, with kind "group".
2. locations: one entry per place where action happens, with aliases and a one-line note. Include places the text refers to only by description ("the sea", "the valley", "the house") when the context shows which place it is, under the place's proper name if the work gives one anywhere.
3. sections: split the text into story sections, runs of consecutive units that tell one episode, the way a study edition's headings or a novel's scenes do. Start a new section when the time, the place or the main action changes. Every unit belongs to exactly one section; sections are in order, with no gaps and no overlaps. This division has 1213 units. Aim for roughly 51 sections (41 to 61), averaging about 24 units each; some sections will be much shorter and some longer. Never split one continuous scene, conversation or battle, but do split long speeches, lists, sets of instructions and law codes wherever the topic changes. Give the ids of each section's first and last unit and a short title. For each section:
   - setting: ids of the locations where its action happens.
   - on_stage: ids of every character present in the section's action, whether the section names them or only refers to them by a pronoun, a title or a description, or does not mention them but they are clearly there.
   - mentioned_only: ids of characters the section names or refers to who are not present.
4. brief: a draft brief for illustrators, for this division only. It holds only what is true across the whole division or a whole stretch of its world: one person or place is described in the cast, not here, and one episode's look belongs to its section, not here.
   - tone: one line on the mood the pictures should carry.
   - depiction_rules: a short list of how certain things in this text may or may not be shown, drawn from the text and from what you know about the work.
   - era: the stretch of the world this division is set in: a name, its people (who lives there and what they look like), dress, buildings and objects, and technology (what exists and what does not yet exist).
   Keep the brief under 200 words.

Use short, stable snake_case ids (for example `david`, `the_queen`, `main_street`). Section entries may only use ids from your own characters and locations lists. Do not quote the text.

characters.name: Moses
characters.note: Hebrew leader raised in Pharaoh's house, son of a Levite mother; flees to Midian, then leads Israel out of Egypt and receives the law at Sinai.

characters.name: Aaron
characters.note: Moses' elder brother and spokesman; becomes the first high priest and makes the golden calf.

characters.name: Pharaoh
characters.note: The Egyptian king who enslaves Israel and resists the plagues; the Pharaoh of the Exodus, whose predecessor (the king who did not know Joseph) is not named.

characters.name: Pharaoh's daughter
characters.note: Finds the infant Moses in the reeds and adopts him; she is unnamed in the text.

characters.name: Miriam
characters.note: Sister of Moses and Aaron; leads the women in song and dance after the sea crossing.

characters.name: Zipporah
characters.note: Midianite wife of Moses, daughter of the priest Jethro (Reuel); circumcises their son at a lodging place.

characters.name: Jethro
characters.note: Priest of Midian and father-in-law of Moses; visits the camp and advises him to appoint judges.

characters.name: Joshua
characters.note: Moses' young assistant; leads the fight against Amalek and stays near the tent of meeting.

characters.name: Bezalel
characters.note: Craftsman filled with the Spirit of God who builds the tabernacle and its furnishings.

characters.name: Oholiab
characters.note: Craftsman who works with Bezalel on the tabernacle, an engraver and embroiderer.

characters.name: Shiphrah and Puah
characters.note: Two Hebrew midwives who defy Pharaoh's order to kill the baby boys; treated as a pair.

characters.name: Moses' mother
aliases: a woman of the house of Levi
characters.note: Hides the infant Moses, floats him in a basket, and is hired back to nurse him; named Jochebed only in genealogy.

characters.name: Moses' sister
characters.note: Watches the basket from afar and arranges the nurse; likely the same as Miriam, identified only by role here.

characters.name: Hur
characters.note: Holds up Moses' hands with Aaron during the battle with Amalek; also named as one left in charge of disputes.

characters.name: The elders of Israel
characters.note: Israelite elders who are gathered, consulted, and go up the mountain with Moses and Aaron.

characters.name: The children of Israel
characters.note: The whole Israelite people who leave Egypt, murmur in the wilderness, and gather at Sinai; acts as one body on stage.

characters.name: The Egyptians
characters.note: Egyptian people, taskmasters, and the army that pursues Israel to the Red Sea.

characters.name: The magicians of Egypt
characters.note: Pharaoh's court magicians who imitate some of Aaron's signs before failing.

characters.name: Yahweh
characters.note: God of Israel who speaks from the burning bush, sends the plagues, and gives the law; appears also as a pillar of cloud and fire.

characters.name: Amalek
characters.note: A people who attack Israel at Rephidim; appear as a group in battle.

characters.name: Nadab and Abihu
characters.note: Sons of Aaron who go up the mountain with the elders; named in the priestly garments section.

locations.name: Egypt
locations.note: The land where Israel is enslaved and the plagues fall.; includes Pharaoh's palace and the cities of storage.; Goshen is the Israelite region within it.

locations.name: Goshen
locations.note: Region of Egypt where Israel dwells, spared from the plagues of flies, hail, and darkness.

locations.name: The river (Nile)
locations.note: The river where the infant Moses is set adrift and where the first plague turns the water to blood.

locations.name: Midian
locations.note: Land where Moses flees, tends Jethro's flock, and receives his call at the mountain of God.

locations.name: Mount Sinai
locations.note: The mountain where Yahweh appears in fire and cloud and gives the law and the tabernacle pattern.

locations.name: The Red Sea
locations.note: The sea that is divided so Israel crosses on dry ground and the Egyptian army drowns.

locations.name: The wilderness
locations.note: The desert between Egypt and the mountain, where Israel wanders, is fed with manna, and finds water.

locations.name: Marah and Elim
locations.note: Stopping places on the desert route, where the water of Marah is made sweet and Elim has springs and palms.

locations.name: Rephidim
locations.note: Camp where Israel lacks water, Moses strikes the rock, and Amalek is defeated.

locations.name: The camp
locations.note: The Israelite encampment in the wilderness, where the golden calf is made and the tent of meeting stands outside.

locations.name: The tabernacle
locations.note: The portable sanctuary built according to the pattern shown on the mountain.

brief.tone: Awe and sacred dread in the plague and mountain scenes, grief and tension in the flight, and warm, devotional calm in the craft and law passages.
depiction_rules: Yahweh is never given a human face or full body; show him as a voice, a burning bush, a pillar of cloud or fire, or the glory filling the tabernacle.
Moses' face shines after Sinai; render as a radiance or veil rather than a literal glow.
The plagues are shown as they occur in the text, with the river blood, swarms, hail, locusts, and darkness, without gratuitous gore beyond the death of the firstborn.
The golden calf is an idol to be shown as a molten calf, not as a god.
The Passover blood on doorposts is shown on lintel and posts only.
Laws and ritual instructions can be shown as objects and settings, not as literal legal scenes.

era.name: Late Bronze Age Egypt, Sinai, and the Sinai wilderness
era.people: Egyptians with shaven heads, linen kilts and wigs, and Hebrew clans in simple desert clothing, dark-haired and bearded; Midianite shepherds.
era.dress: Linen kilts and tunics for Egyptians; plain woven wool and linen for Israelites; priestly garments of blue, purple, scarlet and gold-threaded linen with an ephod, breastplate and bells.
era.buildings_and_objects: Brick storage cities such as Pithom and Raamses for Pharaoh; tents and a portable tabernacle with acacia boards, gold-overlaid ark, lampstand, altars and bronze court; papyrus baskets, clay kneading troughs, rods and staves.
era.technology: Brickmaking with straw and mortar, chariots and horses in the Egyptian army, bronze and gold metalwork, weaving and embroidery, fire and oil lamps; no iron tools, writing on stone tablets, and no coinage (weights are used).
